title: Introduction to Economics
tagline: Wants, resources, scarcity and the questions every economy is forced to answer.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Economics syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (the 2026-27 session syllabus as reproduced by Shaalaa and Jagran Josh; the official cisce.org PDFs were not retrievable). Every question and answer is original practice, no board examination paper was consulted, and no figure is presented as an official statistic.

overview.intro: Economics begins with an uncomfortable fact: human wants are unlimited while the resources available to satisfy them are limited. Every family, firm and government therefore has to choose, and the study of those choices — what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce — is what the subject is about. This chapter builds the foundation the rest of the course stands on: the meaning of an economy and of economic activity, the difference between a want and a need, why scarcity forces choice, and how the three basic questions arise from it. Once these ideas are firm, the chapters on types of economies and on the Indian economy become applications of the same reasoning rather than separate facts to memorise.

learningOutcomes: Define economics in terms of scarcity, wants and resources.
Distinguish wants from needs and resources from goods.
Describe the activities that make up an economy.
Explain why scarcity forces choice at every level.
State the three basic problems every economy must solve.
Recall the definitions of economics attributed to Adams (Adam Smith), Robbins, Keynes and Samuelson, and state what each emphasises.
Distinguish micro from macro economics and economic from non-economic activities with examples.

learn.title: Wants, needs and the first economic fact

blocks.text: A want is a desire for a good or a service: a colder drink on a hot day, a newer pen, a film on Friday. A need is a want whose absence threatens survival or health — food, basic clothing, shelter, elementary medical care. The line between the two moves with circumstance and time: a bicycle is a want for one family and a need for a child who must reach a school three kilometres away. What does not move is the arithmetic. However carefully wants are classified, their number presses against the resources a community has, and that pressure is the starting point of economic reasoning. Economics does not judge wants; it studies what follows from having more of them than means to satisfy.

items: Wants multiply with knowledge and income: what a person has seen, been told or once afforded becomes a want that did not exist before.
Wants compete for the same income, so satisfying one postpones another — the everyday face of economic choice.
Needs are prioritised by survival, but even needs are met through chosen goods: hunger can be met by many foods at many prices.
Every want, once acted on, becomes demand in a market — the bridge between individual desire and the study of markets.

learn.title: Resources and the scarcity that binds them

blocks.text: A resource is anything that can be used to produce a good or a service. Natural resources — land, water, minerals, forests — come from the environment; human resources — labour, skill, enterprise — come from people; and capital resources — tools, machines, buildings, money used to buy them — are themselves produced by earlier work. Resources are limited in quantity and often in quality, and it is their limitation against unlimited wants that economists call scarcity. Scarcity is not poverty and it is not temporary shortage: a rich country is scarce too, because its means, however large, are still means. Scarcity is the permanent condition that makes choice necessary, and every economic problem in the course grows from it.

items.meaning: Anything used to produce a good or service — natural, human or capital.
The condition in which limited resources cannot satisfy unlimited wants.
A tangible item that satisfies a want, such as food or a tool.
An intangible act that satisfies a want, such as teaching or transport.

learn.title: What an economy is, and what people do inside it

blocks.text: An economy is the system of activities by which a community produces, distributes and consumes the goods and services it needs and wants. It includes the farm and the factory, the shop and the bank, the household that decides its budget and the government that builds the road connecting them. Production creates goods and services; distribution moves them to the people who will use them, through markets, wages and trade; consumption is their final use, which ends their economic journey and starts the demand for the next round. A village that feeds itself and a trading nation are both economies — they differ in scale, in specialisation and in how much of their activity passes through markets, not in kind.

blocks.caption: The three economic activities and what each accomplishes
rows: Creates goods and services from resources
A farmer growing wheat; a teacher teaching a class
Moves goods and services to their users
Final use of goods and services, satisfying wants
A family buying and eating bread

blocks.text: Economics is the study of how individuals, firms and governments choose to use scarce resources to satisfy wants. Older definitions emphasised wealth; modern ones emphasise choice, and the reason is scarcity: wealth is one of the scarce things people choose about. The subject divides into the study of small decisions — a household budget, a firm’s pricing, a consumer’s comparison — and the study of aggregates — a nation’s income, its employment, its price level. For Class IX the foundation is the first kind, because the aggregate behaviour of an economy is only the sum of its small decisions made millions of times over. Every later chapter applies this definition to a specific problem.

items: Economics studies choices under constraint, not choices in general — unlimited choice would make it a trivial subject.
The choices studied are made by three kinds of decision-maker: households, firms and the government.
Micro questions look at one market or one decision-maker; macro questions look at the economy as a whole.
Value judgments are held back: economics describes what a choice costs, not what a person ought to want.

learn.title: The questions scarcity forces on every economy

blocks.text: Because resources are limited, every economy must answer three questions, and it must answer them whether it plans them in a ministry or leaves them to markets. What to produce decides which goods and services are made and in what quantity — guns or butter, food or factories, schools or stadiums. How to produce decides the technique: labour-intensive methods that employ many people, or capital-intensive methods that use machines and employ few. For whom to produce decides how the output is shared — who gets the finer goods and who gets the staples, decided in market economies largely by income, and in planned economies more by the state. Every chapter that follows examines how particular economic systems answer these questions and how India answers them.

items.text: A district government has funds for one project: a new market building or a new school wing.
items.note: What to produce — the same scarce resources cannot make both, so one want is postponed.

items.text: A road contractor may dig with a hundred labourers or with three machines.
items.note: How to produce — the choice between labour-intensive and capital-intensive technique, decided by relative costs.

learn.title: Four definitions of economics: wealth, scarcity, administration and choice

blocks.text: The syllabus asks for the definitions of economics attributed to Adams, Robbins, Keynes and Samuelson, and they are best read as a sequence in which the subject progressively widened its own subject-matter. The earliest definition treats economics as the science of wealth: production and exchange of things that have value, an inquiry into how nations grow rich. ICSE Class IX materials give this wealth definition under Adam Smith — the syllabus lists the name as “Adams”, and school textbooks teach the wealth definition with Adam Smith’s name attached, so a student should recognise the definition under either label. The second definition, Lionel Robbins’s, relocates economics from wealth to scarcity: human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. Nothing in Robbins’s definition is about money — an activity qualifies because it involves choice under constraint, and every such choice has an opportunity cost. The third, attributed in school texts to J. M. Keynes, shifts attention to administration: economics studies the administration of scarce means and the determinants of employment and income, which points the subject towards aggregates — how much the economy produces and how many people work. Paul Samuelson’s definition closes the sequence by combining all three concerns: how people and society choose, with or without the use of money, to employ scarce productive resources that have alternative uses, to produce commodities over time and to distribute them for consumption now and in the future. Read together, the four definitions trace the discipline’s growth from wealth, through scarcity, to employment and finally to choice across time — and an answer that quotes one definition without saying what it emphasises has missed the point of being asked for four.

blocks.caption: The four definitions and what each emphasises
rows: Economics is the science of wealth.
Economics studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses.
Economics is a study of the administration of scarce means and the determinants of employment and income.
Economics studies how society employs scarce resources with alternative uses to produce over time and distribute for present and future consumption.
Choice, production and distribution across time

items: Wealth definitions are criticised for ignoring the services of people and for treating economics as a study of things rather than of human choice.
Robbins’s definition is criticised for excluding welfare — a choice can be economically motivated and still harm society, which the definition does not judge.
Keynes’s administration view is criticised as too narrow: economics also studies far more than employment and income.
Samuelson’s definition is generally treated as the most complete because it keeps scarcity, choice and time together.

learn.title: Micro and macro economics, and economic versus non-economic activity

blocks.text: Economics divides by the size of what it studies. Micro economics examines individual units — a household deciding its budget, a firm setting its price, the market for a single good — and its questions are answered by tracing one decision-maker’s response to one price. Macro economics examines aggregates: national income, general price level, total employment, overall output and the balance of payments — the variables whose behaviour no individual unit determines. The two are complementary rather than rival: the price of one onion is micro, the general price level is macro, and policy needs both the particular and the total. A second distinction of the same chapter is by motive. An economic activity is undertaken to earn money or income — wage employment, trade, production for sale. A non-economic activity is undertaken for love, affection, social concern or pleasure without income: a mother teaching her own child, a volunteer cleaning a neighbourhood, a hobbyist playing music. The same act can fall on either side depending on purpose — teaching a student for payment is economic, teaching your own child at home is not — which is why the classification runs on motive, not on the act itself.

From the pinch, three arrows branch out labelled what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce, showing that each question is a consequence of the same constraint.

keyPoints: Wants are desires for goods and services; needs are wants whose absence threatens survival or health.
Resources are limited natural, human and capital inputs used to produce goods and services.
Scarcity is the permanent gap between unlimited wants and limited resources — not poverty and not temporary shortage.
An economy is the system of production, distribution and consumption through which a community lives.
Economics is the study of how scarce resources are chosen to satisfy wants.
Every economy must answer what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.
The how-to-produce question is the choice between labour-intensive and capital-intensive technique.
Scarcity forces choice, and choice has a cost — the foundation of every problem studied in this course.
examFocus: Define economics in the language of scarcity, wants and resources — a definition without scarcity earns half.
Distinguish want from need with a moving example, such as a bicycle for a distant school.
Explain scarcity against the two common errors: it is not poverty, and it is not temporary shortage.
Describe production, distribution and consumption as a connected sequence, not three isolated definitions.
State the three basic problems and show how each grows from the same limited resources.
Use everyday examples — a household budget, a district project — to prove the definitions are understood.

vocabulary.meaning: The gap between unlimited wants and limited resources that forces choice.
vocabulary.context: Scarcity exists in rich and poor economies alike; it is about limits, not about poverty.

vocabulary.meaning: A desire for a good or service that satisfies a wish or a need.
vocabulary.context: Wants multiply with knowledge and income, so scarcity never resolves itself.

vocabulary.meaning: A want whose absence threatens survival or health.
vocabulary.context: Food and shelter are needs; the specific goods that provide them are still chosen.

vocabulary.meaning: Anything used to produce goods and services: natural, human or capital.
vocabulary.context: Land, labour and machines are the three broad classes of resource.

vocabulary.meaning: The creation of goods and services from resources.
vocabulary.context: Production is the first of the three economic activities studied in this chapter.

vocabulary.meaning: The alternative given up when a choice is made.
vocabulary.context: Every choice created by scarcity carries an alternative that is left unchosen.

questions.prompt: Economics is best defined as the study of:
options: How scarce resources are chosen to satisfy wants
How governments collect taxes from citizens
How shares are bought and sold in markets
How to become wealthy as an individual
questions.answer: How scarce resources are chosen to satisfy wants
questions.explanation: The defining conditions of economics are limited resources and unlimited wants, and the subject studies the choices made between them. Taxation, share trading and personal wealth are particular activities inside an economy, not the definition of the subject.
questions.commonMistake: Defining economics as the study of money — money is a tool of the economy, not its subject matter.

questions.prompt: Which of these best illustrates scarcity?
options: A village with enough water for half its fields in a dry season
A shop that has sold out of one brand of soap
A family that cannot afford a luxury car
A student who chooses between two sweets
questions.answer: A village with enough water for half its fields in a dry season
questions.explanation: Scarcity is a resource pressing against competing wants: the same limited water must be divided among all the fields, so choices must be made. A sold-out brand is a temporary shortage, and the luxury example is about income level rather than the general condition of limits.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing scarcity with shortage — a shortage ends when supply catches up; scarcity never ends.

questions.prompt: The three basic problems of any economy arise because:
options: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
Governments cannot collect enough revenue
People prefer leisure to work
Prices keep changing in markets
questions.answer: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
questions.explanation: What to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce are all forced by the same constraint: with unlimited wants against limited resources, choices must be made about content, technique and distribution. The other options describe particular difficulties, not the origin of the three problems.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the three problems to prices or to government revenue rather than to scarcity itself.

questions.prompt: Which activity moves goods and services from producers to the people who use them?
options: Distribution
Production
Consumption
Saving
questions.explanation: Distribution is the set of activities — trade, transport, marketing, wages — that brings goods and services to their users. Production creates them and consumption uses them up; distribution is the bridge between the two.
questions.commonMistake: Treating distribution as production because it happens in shops; retailing moves goods, it does not make them.

questions.prompt: Complete: human wants are ________ while resources are ________ , and this gap is called scarcity.
questions.explanation: The whole subject grows from this asymmetry: wants keep multiplying while the land, labour and capital available to satisfy them stay limited in quantity and quality.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the terms — resources are the limited side, and wants the unlimited side.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a want and a need, with one example of each.
questions.answer: A want is a desire for a particular good or service, such as a colder drink on a hot day, and it may be acted on or postponed. A need is a want whose absence would threaten survival or health, such as food or basic shelter. The specific goods that meet a need are still chosen — hunger can be met by many foods at many prices — so even needs pass through economic choice.
questions.explanation: The distinction rests on consequence, not on importance: postponing a want is uncomfortable, postponing a need is dangerous. Adding that needs are still met through chosen goods shows the classification does not remove them from economics.
questions.commonMistake: Calling needs more expensive wants — the difference is the consequence of doing without, not the price.

questions.prompt: What is an economy? Name its three main activities.
questions.answer: An economy is the system of activities through which a community produces, distributes and consumes the goods and services it needs and wants. Its three main activities are production, which creates goods and services from resources; distribution, which moves them to their users through trade, transport and markets; and consumption, their final use, which satisfies wants and creates fresh demand for the next round.
questions.explanation: The definition should be given as a system of activities rather than as a place, and the three activities named with one line of function each — the function is what shows understanding rather than recall.
questions.commonMistake: Describing an economy as a country or a market — the economy is the pattern of activity, wherever it happens.

questions.prompt: Explain why scarcity exists even in a wealthy country, and what it forces people to do.
questions.answer: Scarcity exists because wants multiply without limit while the resources available to satisfy them — land, labour, capital and enterprise — remain limited in quantity and quality, however large they become. A wealthy country has more resources per person, but its citizens acquire new wants as soon as old ones are met: better housing follows basic housing, faster travel follows basic transport, longer education follows basic literacy. The resources, though larger, are still finite, and time itself is a resource that no income can extend. Because of this permanent gap, every decision-maker in that country — household, firm and government — must still choose. A household still balances rent against travel and savings; a firm still decides between one product line and another; a government still chooses between roads, hospitals and schools at the margin. Wealth changes what is chosen; it never removes the need to choose.
questions.explanation: The answer must defeat the assumption that abundance ends scarcity: show that wants grow with means, that resources and time remain finite, and that choice persists at household, firm and government levels. Concluding that wealth changes the choice rather than removing it completes the argument.
questions.commonMistake: Arguing that rich countries have solved scarcity — they have larger resources, but the same unlimited wants pressing against them.

questions.prompt: A district has funds for either a new market building or a new school wing. Identify the basic problem involved, explain the choice in economic terms, and state what is given up.
questions.answer: The district faces what to produce: the same scarce public funds cannot build both, so one public want must be served and the other postponed. The choice is made at the margin — the district compares the benefit of the market building, which may raise trade and local employment, against the benefit of the school wing, which serves children who currently study in overcrowded rooms. In economic terms, selecting the school wing carries an opportunity cost: the market building that the same money could have built, together with the trade and employment it would have supported. The correct basis for the choice is not which project is good — both are — but which produces the greater benefit given the district’s present condition, and that comparison is exactly what economics teaches. If the district later raises fresh funds, the postponed project returns to the list, because scarcity was reallocated rather than removed.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the problem named (what to produce), the reasoning framed at the margin, and the given-up alternative identified as opportunity cost. The final sentence shows the deeper point: a choice allocates scarcity, it does not end it.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the district’s dilemma without naming the basic problem or the opportunity cost, which is where the marks sit.

questions.prompt: “Scarcity is a condition, not an event.” Explain this statement with reference to shortages and to economic choice.
questions.answer: A shortage is an event: a specific good fails to reach a shelf because of a strike, a failed harvest or a breakdown, and it ends when supply catches up. Scarcity is the standing condition behind every such event: even with no strike and no failure, the same land could grow more wheat or more cotton, the same hour could be spent studying or earning, and the same public rupee could build a road or a clinic. Because the alternative always exists, choice never stops — which is why scarcity cannot be scheduled away or ended by a good harvest. Shortages make scarcity visible, but scarcity is what forces households to budget, firms to prioritise and governments to weigh projects even in prosperous years. Treating scarcity as a condition is what allows economics to reason about normal times instead of only crises.
questions.explanation: The analytical work is the contrast: a shortage is temporary and specific, scarcity is permanent and general. Examples at household, firm and government level prove the condition operates in prosperity too, which is the heart of the statement.
questions.commonMistake: Answering only about shortages and never establishing why scarcity persists when shortages end.

questions.prompt: Which definition of economics is defined by scarcity and alternative uses rather than by wealth?
options: The Robbins definition
The Adam Smith (Adams) definition
The Keynes definition
None of these — all definitions are about wealth
questions.explanation: Robbins defines economics as the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses — scarcity, choice and opportunity cost, with no reference to money or wealth.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the scarcity definition to Samuelson: Samuelson keeps scarcity but adds production and distribution over time, while scarcity alone is Robbins.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between economic and non-economic activities with an example of each.
questions.answer: An economic activity is undertaken to earn money or income: a shopkeeper selling groceries, a worker drawing wages for farm labour, a firm producing goods for sale — the motive is income. A non-economic activity is undertaken for love, affection, social concern or pleasure without any income in view: a mother teaching her own child, a volunteer distributing food, someone gardening as a hobby. The same act can belong to either category depending on motive — teaching a student in school for fees is economic, teaching your own child at home is not — so the classification turns on purpose rather than on the act itself.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both definitions by motive plus one example each, and the closing observation that motive decides the classification — that is the point the distinction is testing.
questions.commonMistake: Classifying by whether money changes hands in that particular instance rather than by purpose — the same act can be economic or non-economic.
